slides.text:
Cobra builds command-line programs: tools you run from the terminal by name, like `git status`. Every action is a **command**, a plain Go value with a name, a description and a function to run.

The snippet is pseudo code, not Go.
slides.code:
command:
    name: hello
    description: says hello
    action: print a greeting

slides.text:
Two sessions:

- **Session 1:** build a command, give it an action and start it
- **Session 2:** describe it with `Short`, `Long` and `Use`, and declare it as the root of the program

A command is described by a `cobra.Command` struct. Three fields are enough to start:

- `Use`: the name
- `Short`: a one-line description
- `Run`: the function that does the work
`Run` is a function with two parameters. `cmd` is the command being run, and `args` holds the extra words typed after its name. This module leaves `args` alone.

Building a command does nothing by itself. `Execute` reads what the user typed and runs the command. It returns an error, and `main` turns that into an exit code: 1 means failure.

The snippet is pseudo code, not Go.
slides.code:
Execute:
    read the command line
    find the command
    run its Run function
    return an error if it failed

slides.text:
Every command has two descriptions. `Short` is a single line. `Long` is a fuller text, shown in the command's own help.

The fields of the struct are ordinary values, so a `Run` function can read them through `cmd`.
Only the first word of `Use` is the name. Whatever follows is a hint about the arguments the command takes. `cmd.Name()` returns just the first word.
Real programs declare the root command as a package-level variable, so `main` only has to start it. A package-level variable uses `var`, because `:=` works only inside functions.
